definition: To spread an idea, belief, or piece of information to more and more people.
example: Old textbooks helped propagate the myth that people use only ten percent of their brains.
nuance: Propagate stresses spreading something so it multiplies and reaches more people; promulgate means announcing it officially.
prompt: A rumor that the class field trip has been canceled is moving through a middle school.
options: Group chats helped propagate the rumor until most of the grade believed the trip was off.
The principal's announcement propagated the rumor by proving it false and ending the gossip.
Maya chose to propagate the rumor by keeping it entirely to herself.
The vice principal propagated each student to learn who had started the story.
reasons: Passing a claim from person to person until it reaches many people is exactly the spreading meant.
Disproving a story and stopping its spread is the reverse of what the word describes.
Something kept private is never passed along, so nothing spreads.
The word does not mean questioning people; that sense belongs to interrogate.

practice.prompt: A historian discovers that a famous quotation was never actually said by anyone.
options: The archivist propagated the quotation by checking its date against old newspapers.
Quote websites still propagate the invented line, each copying it from the others.
The historian propagated the quotation by publishing evidence that no one had ever said it.
Desmond propagated the famous line for his own speech and claimed he had written it.
reasons: Checking when words first appeared is verification; it passes them to no one new.
Copying the false line from site to site keeps it reaching new readers, which is spreading it.
Exposing a claim as false works against its spread rather than helping it along.
Taking credit for someone else's words is appropriating, a look-alike with a different meaning.
